power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

info.title: Five Platform Functions and the Frustration-Aggression Pathway: A Mechanism Model of Grievance Identity Formation among Young Men

text.text: Aggression research holds that aversive experience raises aggressive readiness, but whether aggression is enacted depends on appraisal, cue exposure, reinforcement, and inhibition.
This theory article specifies how digital platforms may modulate that pathway for young men exposed to identity-relevant status threat.

It disaggregates platform effects into five functions: a social comparison amplifier, an identity threat accelerator, a cue-saturated environment, a reinforcement architecture, and an aggression affordance system.

Each maps onto a component of the General Aggression Model, cognitive neoassociationism, or I³ Theory, and each is paired with a discriminant prediction that would count against that function if it failed.

The article defines grievance identity as a self-schema marked by central in-group injustice, chronically accessible hostile attributions, legitimised adversarial behaviour, and peer recognition for hostile performance, and distinguishes it from collective victimhood, identity fusion, and ideological commitment.
A six-stage pathway links identity-relevant goal blockage to inhibition erosion.
The article engages with contested evidence on algorithmic recommendation, the selectionversus-amplification identification problem, and the generalisation gap in precarious manhood research.
It reports no data and sets out an empirical agenda and conditions for falsification.

Aggression research is organised around a central proposition: aversive experience increases aggressive readiness, but whether aggression is enacted depends on appraisal, cue activation, reinforcement, and restraint (Anderson & Bushman, 2002; Berkowitz, 1989 Berkowitz, , 1990;; Finkel, 2014).
text.formatted: Aggression research is organised around a central proposition: aversive experience increases aggressive readiness, but whether aggression is enacted depends on appraisal, cue activation, reinforcement, and restraint <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Anderson & Bushman, 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Berkowitz, 1989</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Berkowitz, , 1990;;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Finkel, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: The environments in which frustration unfolds have changed.

For many young men, daily social evaluation now takes place in algorithmically curated digital settings that offer frequent social comparison, public metrics of status, dense hostile or contemptuous content, intermittent social reward, and weak accountability.
These settings introduce no new human motives.
They alter exposure frequency, evaluative salience, and feedback contingencies, which are the parameters that aggression models emphasise.
Aggression frameworks have been applied to digital contexts before (Allen, Anderson, & Bushman, 2018; Kowalski et al., 2014; Suler, 2004).
text.formatted: Aggression frameworks have been applied to digital contexts before <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Allen, Anderson, & Bushman, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Kowalski et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Suler, 2004)</ref>.

text.text: This article goes one step further by disaggregating 'platform effects' into five functions that can be separated conceptually and, in principle, empirically.

Each function maps onto a component of existing aggression theory, and each is paired with a discriminant prediction: a claim that follows from that function and not from the other four, so that a failed prediction counts against the function rather than against the framework as a whole.
The article also defines grievance identity as the endpoint of a staged pathway, distinguishes it from neighbouring constructs, and proposes ways to measure it.

The focus on young men follows from research on precarious manhood, which holds that manhood is construed as earned and socially revocable (Vandello, Bosson, Cohen, Burnaford, & Weaver, 2008; Vandello & Bosson, 2013).
text.formatted: The focus on young men follows from research on precarious manhood, which holds that manhood is construed as earned and socially revocable <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Vandello, Bosson, Cohen, Burnaford, & Weaver, 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Vandello & Bosson, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: The claim is contingent and not essentialist: masculinity threat sensitivity is treated as a moderator, and the model is probabilistic.
The article is a theory paper.
It reports no data, and its predictions are offered for testing.
A companion article develops a sociological account of the institutional conditions under which these processes arise (Verheyden, 2026).
text.formatted: A companion article develops a sociological account of the institutional conditions under which these processes arise <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Verheyden, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Classical formulation and revision Dollard, Doob, Miller, Mowrer, and Sears (1939) proposed that frustration, the interference with goal-directed behaviour, produces an instigation to aggression.
text.formatted: Classical formulation and revision <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Dollard, Doob, Miller, Mowrer, and Sears (1939)</ref> proposed that frustration, the interference with goal-directed behaviour, produces an instigation to aggression.

text.text: The strong form was soon found wanting: people often respond to blocked goals with withdrawal, self-blame, or renewed problem-solving, and aggression can be instrumental and occur without frustration (Anderson & Bushman, 2002; Berkowitz, 1989).
text.formatted: The strong form was soon found wanting: people often respond to blocked goals with withdrawal, self-blame, or renewed problem-solving, and aggression can be instrumental and occur without frustration <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Anderson & Bushman, 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Berkowitz, 1989)</ref>.

text.text: The tradition then moved from inevitability to conditional, process-based models.
It also became clear that frustration is heterogeneous.
A thwarted convenience goal differs from humiliation, relational rejection, or perceived injustice (Berkowitz, 1990 (Berkowitz, , 1993)).
text.formatted: A thwarted convenience goal differs from humiliation, relational rejection, or perceived injustice <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Berkowitz, 1990</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Berkowitz, , 1993))</ref>.

text.text: Many platform-mediated frustrations are repeated evaluative microfailures in the domains of status and belonging, and for these it is the aversive affect and appraisal they generate that matter, more than the event category. Berkowitz (1989 Berkowitz ( , 1990) ) replaced inevitability with an affect-mediated, cue-dependent process.
text.formatted: Many platform-mediated frustrations are repeated evaluative microfailures in the domains of status and belonging, and for these it is the aversive affect and appraisal they generate that matter, more than the event category. <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Berkowitz (1989</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Berkowitz ( , 1990) )</ref> replaced inevitability with an affect-mediated, cue-dependent process.

text.text: Aversive events generate negative affect, negative affect activates associative networks of aggressive thoughts, feelings, and action tendencies, and the likelihood of aggression depends on the availability of aggression-relevant cues and scripts.

Two implications carry over to platforms: chronic low-grade aversive experience can raise aggressive readiness, and the direction of aggression is shaped by what is present in the environment and accessible in memory.
The General Aggression Model (GAM) integrates affective, cognitive, and learning traditions.
Person and situation inputs act through cognition, affect, and arousal, followed by appraisal and decision processes.
The model is cyclical, in that each episode is a learning trial that can change the accessibility of aggressive knowledge structures (Anderson & Bushman, 2002; DeWall, Anderson, & Bushman, 2011).
text.formatted: The model is cyclical, in that each episode is a learning trial that can change the accessibility of aggressive knowledge structures <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Anderson & Bushman, 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">DeWall, Anderson, & Bushman, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: I³ Theory states that aggression is most likely when instigation is strong, impellance is strong, and inhibition is weak (Finkel, 2014).
text.formatted: I³ Theory states that aggression is most likely when instigation is strong, impellance is strong, and inhibition is weak <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Finkel, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Its value here is its demand for precision: a claim that 'platforms increase aggression' is not mechanismlevel, and one must say which platform features raise instigation, which raise impellance, and which weaken inhibition.
The frustration-aggression link is strongest when aversive experience is appraised as unjust, identity-relevant, and attributable to others.

Research on masculinity threat gives a mechanism-level account of why some frustrations, notably those involving romantic desirability and public standing, can produce anger and compensatory aggression among men under certain cultural conditions (Vandello et al., 2008; Vandello & Bosson, 2013).
text.formatted: Research on masculinity threat gives a mechanism-level account of why some frustrations, notably those involving romantic desirability and public standing, can produce anger and compensatory aggression among men under certain cultural conditions <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Vandello et al., 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Vandello & Bosson, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: The evidence base for precarious manhood theory is mainly laboratory work with mild threat manipulations and student samples, such as feedback implying failure on a masculine task.
The outcomes include risk-taking, dominance displays, and endorsement of aggression.
These are not equivalent to the sustained online harassment, coordinated hostile campaigns, or grievance identity formation theorised here.
Three considerations narrow the gap without closing it.
The core mechanism, threat-sensitive activation of compensatory motivation, is theoretically continuous with status threat outside the laboratory.
Qualitative work on manosphere communities describes masculinity as a recurring response to threat (Ging, 2019).
text.formatted: Qualitative work on manosphere communities describes masculinity as a recurring response to threat <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Ging, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: And reviews of cyberaggression research link rejection sensitivity and identity to online hostility, although causal attribution is limited (Kowalski et al., 2014).
text.formatted: And reviews of cyberaggression research link rejection sensitivity and identity to online hostility, although causal attribution is limited <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Kowalski et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: The model therefore treats precariousmanhood mechanisms as theoretically motivated, partly supported, and underdetermined at the naturalistic level, and it makes masculinity threat sensitivity a moderator and not a populationlevel predictor.
Social comparison theory holds that people evaluate themselves against others, especially when objective standards are ambiguous (Festinger, 1954).
text.formatted: Social comparison theory holds that people evaluate themselves against others, especially when objective standards are ambiguous <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Festinger, 1954)</ref>.

text.text: Relative deprivation theory adds that perceived disadvantage produces resentment when it is seen as unfair or externally caused (Runciman, 1966; Walker & Smith, 2002).
text.formatted: Relative deprivation theory adds that perceived disadvantage produces resentment when it is seen as unfair or externally caused <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Runciman, 1966;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Walker & Smith, 2002)</ref>.

text.text: Collective victimhood research shows how personal frustration can be reframed as group injustice, which externalises causes and supplies moral justification for hostility (Noor, Shnabel, Halabi, & Nadler, 2012). Bandura's (1999) account of moral disengagement lists the mechanisms through which people deactivate moral self-sanctions: moral justification, euphemistic labelling, diffusion of responsibility, dehumanisation, and attribution of blame.
text.formatted: Collective victimhood research shows how personal frustration can be reframed as group injustice, which externalises causes and supplies moral justification for hostility <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Noor, Shnabel, Halabi, & Nadler, 2012)</ref>. <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Bandura's (1999)</ref> account of moral disengagement lists the mechanisms through which people deactivate moral self-sanctions: moral justification, euphemistic labelling, diffusion of responsibility, dehumanisation, and attribution of blame.

text.text: In grievance communities these can be collectively scaffolded and socially rewarded.
Suler (2004) identified dissociative anonymity, invisibility, asynchronicity, and the minimisation of authority as factors that increase disinhibited online behaviour.
This corresponds to the inhibition component of I³ Theory.
Disinhibition and moral disengagement are distinct: the first removes situational constraints and the second removes internal ones.
The model predicts that they interact multiplicatively, with moral disengagement making hostile behaviour feel justified and disinhibition making it feel free of consequences.
Table 1 summarises the five functions, the platform feature each identifies, the aggression-theory component it maps onto, and its discriminant prediction.
text.formatted: Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref> summarises the five functions, the platform feature each identifies, the aggression-theory component it maps onto, and its discriminant prediction.

text.text: They are not alternative labels for one process.
A platform can have any combination of the features.

A professional networking site, for example, may have high comparison salience and visible metrics with little hostile content, and an anonymous image board may have high disinhibition with little comparison.
This variability is what makes the taxonomy empirically tractable.

Feeds, influencer ecologies, and curated streams expose users repeatedly to upward comparison targets, and dating interfaces quantify desirability so that relational standing feels ranked and not contextual.

Research on social media and comparison finds associations with negative self-evaluation, but effects are modest and heterogeneous, and the usual outcome is depressive affect or lower self-esteem rather than hostility (Appel, Gerlach, & Crusius, 2016; Vogel, Rose, Roberts, & Eckles, 2014).
text.formatted: Research on social media and comparison finds associations with negative self-evaluation, but effects are modest and heterogeneous, and the usual outcome is depressive affect or lower self-esteem rather than hostility <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Appel, Gerlach, & Crusius, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Vogel, Rose, Roberts, & Eckles, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: The model therefore places this function in the production of chronic negative affect and perceived status loss, which feed Berkowitz-type associative activation and GAM's affective route.
It is an instigation-raising mechanism and not an aggression mechanism in itself.

Comparison frequency and evaluative salience, measured through content exposure and not through time on platform, should predict negative affect intensity and instigation frequency, with metric visibility, content density, feedback variability, and anonymity controlled.
A finding that comparison salience predicts negative affect only through metric visibility would challenge the independence of this function.
Platforms turn diffuse social standing into visible metrics: likes, follower counts, view totals, match frequencies.
Metrics make social evaluation explicit and numerically legible and so raise the diagnosticity of comparison.

For men under precarious-manhood conditions, repeated public markers of failure, such as romantic non-selection or invisibility, can be appraised as threats that call for compensation through dominance displays (Vandello et al., 2008).
text.formatted: For men under precarious-manhood conditions, repeated public markers of failure, such as romantic non-selection or invisibility, can be appraised as threats that call for compensation through dominance displays <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Vandello et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: The distinction from the comparison function is that this one concerns the public legibility and revisability of feedback and not its frequency.

Metric visibility (the degree to which status indicators are public, quantified, and revisable) should predict compensatory aggressive motivation among men high in threat sensitivity, independently of comparison frequency.
A dating-app experiment could deliver equivalent match-rate feedback either privately or in public rankings.
Under Berkowitz's account, negative affect raises readiness but cues determine which networks and scripts are activated.
Recommendation systems, community clustering, and engagement-based sorting can provide sustained, semantically coherent cue sets.
The strength of this claim must be set against contested evidence.

Audits of YouTube have reported pathways towards more extreme content for some users (Ribeiro, Ottoni, West, Almeida, & Meira, 2020), while other work finds that consumption of radical content is concentrated among a small group who actively seek it (Hosseinmardi, Ghasemian, Clauset, Mobius, Rothschild, & Watts, 2021).
text.formatted: Audits of YouTube have reported pathways towards more extreme content for some users <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Ribeiro, Ottoni, West, Almeida, & Meira, 2020)</ref>, while other work finds that consumption of radical content is concentrated among a small group who actively seek it <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Hosseinmardi, Ghasemian, Clauset, Mobius, Rothschild, & Watts, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: A large experiment during the 2020 US election found that reducing exposure to like-minded sources on Facebook did not measurably change polarisation (Nyhan et al., 2023), and exposure to opposing views on social media can increase polarisation (Bail et al., 2018).
text.formatted: A large experiment during the 2020 US election found that reducing exposure to like-minded sources on Facebook did not measurably change polarisation <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Nyhan et al., 2023)</ref>, and exposure to opposing views on social media can increase polarisation <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Bail et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: These findings require the framework to be stated carefully.
It should not be put as 'algorithms push users towards hostile content'.

The defensible claim is that platform architecture, through community clustering, engagement-based sorting, and search, creates accessible cue ecologies that users who are already seeking grievance-consistent material can inhabit efficiently.
The mechanism is userdriven grievance-seeking facilitated by architecture, and algorithmic push is a possible contributor and not a premise.

The semantic density of hostile or contemptuous material that users actually encounter, measured by computational text analysis of browsing logs or content diaries and not inferred from time on platform, should predict hostile script accessibility and hostile attribution bias under negative affect, over and above comparison frequency and metric salience.
Intermittent reinforcement, particularly on variable-ratio schedules, produces persistent responding (Ferster & Skinner, 1957).
text.formatted: Intermittent reinforcement, particularly on variable-ratio schedules, produces persistent responding <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Ferster & Skinner, 1957)</ref>.

text.text: If hostile posts attract more engagement for some users in some contexts, they may be reinforced, and reinforcement shapes expectations about what works and consolidates hostile expression as a script.
The translation from laboratory schedules to social media needs qualification.
Social feedback involves many co-agents, heterogeneous audiences, and diffuse timing.

The analogy is treated here as a structural homology: feedback that resembles variable-ratio schedules in its unpredictability and immediacy should produce similar persistence effects, even if the underlying processes differ.

Social rejection and social reward engage neural systems overlapping with those of physical pain and reward (Eisenberger & Lieberman, 2004), which makes the claim more than rhetorical, although the step from individual neural response to population behaviour requires caution.
text.formatted: Social rejection and social reward engage neural systems overlapping with those of physical pain and reward <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Eisenberger & Lieberman, 2004)</ref>, which makes the claim more than rhetorical, although the step from individual neural response to population behaviour requires caution.

text.text: The distinctive implication is persistence without acute affect.
A user who is not currently angry may keep producing hostile content if it has been intermittently rewarded with attention and in-group approval.

Feedback schedule variability, measured as within-person variance in post-level engagement for hostile posts, should predict the persistence of hostile expression independently of current negative affect, comparison exposure, or content density.
I³ Theory stresses inhibition, and online disinhibition specifies why inhibition may be weaker in many digital settings.

Research on cyberaggression finds associations between anonymity and aggressive behaviour, with effects that vary by platform and are moderated by norm climate and enforcement (Kowalski et al., 2014).
text.formatted: Research on cyberaggression finds associations between anonymity and aggressive behaviour, with effects that vary by platform and are moderated by norm climate and enforcement <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Kowalski et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Governance studies provide naturalistic evidence on the restoring side.

After Reddit banned two large hate communities in 2015, users who had been active in them and stayed on the platform substantially reduced their hate speech (Chandrasekharan, Pavalanathan, Srinivasan, Glynn, Eisenstein, & Gilbert, 2017).
text.formatted: After Reddit banned two large hate communities in 2015, users who had been active in them and stayed on the platform substantially reduced their hate speech <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Chandrasekharan, Pavalanathan, Srinivasan, Glynn, Eisenstein, & Gilbert, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: This is the kind of quasi-experimental evidence that helps to separate enforcement effects from selection, though one ban on one platform does not establish general effects.

Perceived accountability, measured through perceived anonymity, anticipated moderation, and norm-climate perceptions, should moderate the probability of enactment independently of affect, attribution, and script accessibility, given equivalent urge strength.
This can be tested in I³-consistent factorial designs in which instigation and impellance are fixed and accountability is varied.
The functions can come apart.
A leaderboard-based trading platform would combine high comparison and high metric visibility with little hostile content, predicting threat and negative affect without script-based hostility.
An anonymous image board would combine high disinhibition and community-level moral disengagement with dense hostile cues, predicting enactment without a comparison-driven path.
A fitness-tracking platform would have high comparison with non-hostile cues and strong accountability, predicting negative affect without script activation.
A heavily moderated political forum would have dense cues but restored inhibition, predicting reduced enactment despite high engagement.
These contrasts are predictions and have not been tested.
Research that treats all platforms as instances of 'social media use' will not detect function-specific effects.
One of the five functions, the cue-saturated environment, can be illustrated with the sockpuppet audit by Baker et al. (2024).
text.formatted: One of the five functions, the cue-saturated environment, can be illustrated with the sockpuppet audit by <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Baker et al. (2024)</ref>.

text.text: The study ran ten accounts on blank smartphones, five on TikTok and five on YouTube Shorts.
On each platform, a 16-year-old and an 18-year-old sought gender-normative content, a 16-year-old and an 18-year-old sought manosphere content, and a control did not engage.
The YouTube Shorts accounts were registered as male; TikTok does not ask for gender at sign-up.

Each account viewed eight rounds of 50 videos from the main feed, the researchers watched and liked problematic videos when these were served, and the recordings were manually coded into categories that included alpha masculinity, misogyny and anti-feminism, reactionary right, and conspiracy content (Baker et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Each account viewed eight rounds of 50 videos from the main feed, the researchers watched and liked problematic videos when these were served, and the recordings were manually coded into categories that included alpha masculinity, misogyny and anti-feminism, reactionary right, and conspiracy content <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Baker et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: The cue-saturation prediction concerns the semantic density of hostile material that users actually encounter.
The audit measures exactly this on the supply side.
Every account that sought gender-normative or manosphere content was shown toxic content within 23 minutes and manosphere content within 26 minutes.
By the final round, about three-quarters of recommended videos were coded toxic on both platforms (76 per cent on TikTok and 78 per cent on YouTube Shorts).

Over all rounds the average was 61.5 per cent on YouTube Shorts and 34.7 per cent on TikTok, and manosphere content made up 56 per cent of recommendations on YouTube Shorts and 21.1 per cent on TikTok.

On YouTube Shorts accounts that sought manosphere content received more toxic content than those that did not (71.4 per cent against 51.6 per cent), whereas on TikTok the difference was small (32.5 and 36.6 per cent) (Baker et al., 2024).
text.formatted: On YouTube Shorts accounts that sought manosphere content received more toxic content than those that did not (71.4 per cent against 51.6 per cent), whereas on TikTok the difference was small (32.5 and 36.6 per cent) <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Baker et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: The audit PLATFORM FUNCTIONS AND AGGRESSION 13 therefore shows high and variable cue density that differs by platform and, on YouTube Shorts, by the user's signalled interest.
Because the researchers engaged with problematic videos when served, the rise across rounds reflects density under engagement and not density for a disengaged user.
The audit is silent on the other four functions and on every outcome.

It did not measure social comparison, metric visibility, the reinforcement schedule of a user's own posts, or perceived accountability, and it measured no affect, attribution, or aggression, since the accounts are simulations.
It also leaves selection and amplification unseparated: the accounts that sought manosphere content were assigned to do so by the researchers.

Its small size, short duration, and manual coding, with inter-coder testing described but no reliability statistic reported, and no toxic-content results reported for the control accounts, limit what can be generalised (Baker et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Its small size, short duration, and manual coding, with inter-coder testing described but no reliability statistic reported, and no toxic-content results reported for the control accounts, limit what can be generalised <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Baker et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: What the audit contributes is a measurement approach for the independent variable in the cue-saturation prediction, which can be combined with the user-level designs described below, such as donated browsing data, in which the density of hostile material encountered is linked to affect and attribution measures.
The staged pathway below ends in a construct that earlier accounts leave underspecified.

Grievance identity is a self-schema in which (a) perceived injustice directed at the in-group is central to identity, (b) hostile attributions towards designated outgroups are chronically accessible, (c) adversarial behaviour is experienced as legitimate and identity-affirming, and (d) recognition from in-group peers for hostile performance functions as status restoration and not merely as reward.
It is distinct from three neighbours.
Collective victimhood (Noor et al., 2012) is a grouplevel perception of shared harm, whereas grievance identity is an individual self-schema that may or may not rest on actual collective harm.
text.formatted: Collective victimhood <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Noor et al., 2012)</ref> is a grouplevel perception of shared harm, whereas grievance identity is an individual self-schema that may or may not rest on actual collective harm.

text.text: Identity fusion (Swann, Gómez, Seyle, Morales, & Huici, 2009) concerns the intensity of identification with a group, whereas grievance identity concerns the hostile content of that identification.
text.formatted: Identity fusion <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Swann, Gómez, Seyle, Morales, & Huici, 2009)</ref> concerns the intensity of identification with a group, whereas grievance identity concerns the hostile content of that identification.

text.text: Ideological commitment concerns explicit beliefs about social organisation, whereas grievance identity operates at the level of self-concept and behavioural readiness and can exist without a coherent ideology.

Four components can be assessed: the centrality of in-group victimhood to self-concept, using adapted items from identity-centrality scales (Luhtanen & Crocker, 1992); hostile attribution towards designated outgroups, using scenario-based tasks adapted from hostile attribution bias measures; endorsement of retaliatory norms; and self-reported willingness to act adversarially in defence of in-group standing.
text.formatted: Four components can be assessed: the centrality of in-group victimhood to self-concept, using adapted items from identity-centrality scales <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Luhtanen & Crocker, 1992)</ref>; hostile attribution towards designated outgroups, using scenario-based tasks adapted from hostile attribution bias measures; endorsement of retaliatory norms; and self-reported willingness to act adversarially in defence of in-group standing.

text.text: These correspond to the definition and could be tested for discriminant validity against collective victimhood and identity fusion with structural equation methods.
No measure has been developed or validated here.
A mechanism model should specify ordering, mediators, moderators, and feedback.
The pathway has six stages, each tied to constructs that can be measured, and each transition yields a mediational prediction.
Most people who enter the early stages will not pass through all six.
Stage 1: identity-relevant goal blockage as chronic instigation.
Platforms can generate frequent micro-failures: relational non-selection, invisibility, unfavourable comparisons, and low status metrics.
These are chronic instigators that accumulate into stable aversive affect (Finkel, 2014).
text.formatted: These are chronic instigators that accumulate into stable aversive affect <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Finkel, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Many people respond with sadness or withdrawal, and appraisal determines whether the pathway continues.
Stage 2: arousal and shame-anger conversion.
Identity-relevant failure often produces shame, which is self-focused and inhibits action, before it produces anger, which is otherdirected and favours approach.
The conversion of shame into anger is a pivotal point.
Precarious manhood theory suggests why it may be more likely where status is tied to dominance: anger supports confrontation, and shame supports withdrawal.
The model does not hold that men naturally convert shame to anger.

It holds that where threatened status is linked to expectations of dominance, anger is a culturally legible route to restoration, more accessible where environments supply external attribution frames and validating communities.
The mechanism of conversion needs further theoretical and empirical grounding.
Stage 3: attributional framing.
Grievance narratives supply templates that interpret setbacks as externally caused and unjust, which raises hostile attribution bias (Noor et al., 2012; Runciman, 1966; Walker & Smith, 2002).
text.formatted: Grievance narratives supply templates that interpret setbacks as externally caused and unjust, which raises hostile attribution bias <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Noor et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Runciman, 1966;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Walker & Smith, 2002)</ref>.

text.text: Attribution supplies targets and moral logic, whereas cue exposure supplies triggers and scripts.
Someone can meet many hostile cues without adopting a frame, or hold a strong frame from offline sources with little cue exposure.
The model predicts that both are needed for full progression and that their conjunction matters more than either alone.
Stage 4: cue activation and script retrieval.
Under negative affect and a hostile attributional frame, cues activate aggressive networks.

Cues need not be violent; repeated contempt frames, dehumanising labels, and moralised antagonism can operate (Berkowitz, 1990), and repeated exposure may raise the long-term accessibility of aggressive scripts (Anderson & Bushman, 2002).
text.formatted: Cues need not be violent; repeated contempt frames, dehumanising labels, and moralised antagonism can operate <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Berkowitz, 1990)</ref>, and repeated exposure may raise the long-term accessibility of aggressive scripts <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Anderson & Bushman, 2002)</ref>.

text.text: Reinforcement explains why hostile behaviour can persist without resolving the frustration.
If hostile performance is rewarded within a community, it becomes a strategy for status restoration.
Validation confirms the grievance frame and encourages interpretation of later setbacks through the same lens.
This is the transition from episodic anger to grievance identity, in which hostile performance becomes constitutive of the self, and it is where the four components defined above consolidate.
Disinhibition and moral disengagement weaken restraint, and peers can supply justifications and contempt language.
This can move behaviour from episodic enactment under low inhibition to a broader reduction in restraint, and under specific high-risk conditions the change may generalise offline.
Across cycles, aggressive episodes act as learning trials.

For some individuals in some environments, repeated cycles under high instigation, high impellance, low inhibition, and social reinforcement may produce trait-like change in hostile attribution and in the accessibility of aggressive scripts.
This is a predicted possibility and not an inevitability.
The model's outcomes are conditional.
Moderators include masculinity threat sensitivity, offline embedding and cross-cutting ties, platform governance and enforcement, and norm climate.
Embedding in work, education, and varied relationships supplies competing frames and reputational costs for hostility.
The central identification problem is selection versus amplification.
People who are already hostile or aggrieved may seek out grievance communities, and the association between platform exposure and hostility may reflect selection and not effect.
Evidence that radical content consumption is concentrated among those who seek it (Hosseinmardi et al., 2021) means that selection must be taken seriously and cannot be assumed away.
text.formatted: Evidence that radical content consumption is concentrated among those who seek it <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Hosseinmardi et al., 2021)</ref> means that selection must be taken seriously and cannot be assumed away.

text.text: The model's position is that selection and amplification are not alternatives: users with chronic negative affect and identity threat are more likely to seek grievance-consistent material, and platform architecture and reinforcement may then deepen and consolidate what selection started.
This position is only plausible until designs separate the two.

Needed designs include panel studies with pre-exposure measures, within-person analyses of changes after governance shifts or exposure, and natural experiments such as platform bans or algorithm changes.
The model yields six propositions, five from the platform functions and one from the staged pathway.
Comparison frequency and evaluative salience predict negative affect and instigation frequency independently of metric visibility, content density, and feedback variability.
Public, quantified status indicators predict compensatory aggressive motivation among men high in threat sensitivity, independently of comparison frequency.
The semantic density of hostile material actually encountered predicts hostile script accessibility and attribution bias under negative affect, over and above comparison and metric salience.
The framework would be weakened by several kinds of finding.
If the five predicted effects collapse into one latent factor, so that the functions cannot be separated empirically, the taxonomy would not be doing the work claimed.
If reinforcement variability does not predict persistence once affect is controlled, the persistence-without-affect claim fails.
If perceived accountability does not moderate enactment at fixed urge strength, the affordance function fails.
If panel studies show no progression from early to late stages beyond what pre-exposure traits predict, selection would be favoured over amplification.
This is a theory paper without data, and its literature was selected by the author and not through a systematic search.
Several of the empirical studies it relies on are laboratory studies, specific to one platform or period, or disputed.
The generalisation gap from precarious-manhood experiments to naturalistic behaviour is acknowledged, not closed.
The reinforcement analogy is a structural homology, and the shame-anger conversion is the least-developed link in the pathway.
The five functions may overlap more in practice than in theory.
The grievance identity construct has been defined but not measured.

Alternative accounts remain open: that selection explains most of the observed association, that offline social conditions drive both platform use and hostility, or that a single mechanism such as reinforcement does most of the work.
The model should be read as a set of testable claims and should not be taken as a finding.
It also does not imply that aggression is common among men who experience frustration or use these platforms.
Most do not progress along the pathway.

Progression from early to late stages of the pathway is predicted by cumulative exposure to the five functions beyond what pre-exposure traits predict.
If it is not, selection is favoured over amplification.
Research Agenda Testing the model requires measures of each function that are independent of the others and of generic platform use.
Computational text analysis of browsing logs, content diaries, or donated data can estimate the semantic density of hostile material encountered.
Digital trace data can estimate metric visibility and within-person variance in engagement feedback.

Experiments can vary the public or private delivery of equivalent feedback (identity threat), the schedule of rewards for hostile versus neutral expression (reinforcement), and perceived accountability (affordance).
Platform audits can examine what recommendation systems and search return for accounts at different stages, with attention to the limits of sockpuppet designs, which do not measure effects on users.
Natural experiments, such as bans, changes in metric display, and changes to recommendation logic, offer leverage on the amplification question.
Panel studies can estimate the transitions between stages and test the mediational predictions.

Its value is in making disagreement empirical: each function says what should be measured and what outcome would refute it.

Whether the model survives will depend on designs that separate selection from amplification and that measure content, metrics, feedback, and accountability directly and not through generic platform use.
